openers.circular-and-bio-based-economies: Most things people buy follow a one-way road: dug up, made, used and thrown away. This chapter is about the alternatives, starting with recycling, which turns waste materials into new materials and objects. From there the ideas widen into whole systems: an economy that keeps products, parts and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible, and a ranking of ways to deal with waste, usually drawn as a pyramid. Some of the answers are about firms and habits, such as sharing goods through online platforms or making more with less material. Others are about doubt, because critics ask whether recycling pays and whether keeping materials in loops leaves growth itself unquestioned.

nature-eecon-038.title: Recycling: giving waste a second life
nature-eecon-038.text:
Melting down an old aluminium can takes only 5% of the energy needed to make aluminium from scratch. That gap explains much of the appeal of recycling, the turning of waste materials into new materials and objects. Two-thirds of all new steel is estimated to come from recycled steel.

Recycling is the third step in the familiar 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' hierarchy. It saves materials and energy. It also cuts greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution from incineration and water pollution from landfills, all forms of {{ref:nature-found-079}}.

The ideal is a loop in which a material becomes a fresh supply of the same material, as metal cans can. For many materials that is hard or costly, so they become different, lesser products instead. Much of the difficulty starts at the drawing board: products are often not designed to be recycled. In the USA only about 6 to 7 percent of plastic is recycled.

Money drove the first big push. Large investment in recycling came in the 1970s, when rising energy costs made saving energy pay.

nature-eecon-001.title: Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste
nature-eecon-001.text:
Extracting and processing material resources accounts for over 55 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. The usual economy treats those materials as a one-way flow: extract them, use them, throw them away. Critics call this the linear 'take-make-waste' economy, and it puts heavy pressure on the environment.

A circular economy is the alternative. It is an {{ref:nature-econ-153}} that tries to keep products, parts and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible. The European Parliament describes it as sharing, leasing, reusing, repairing, refurbishing and recycling existing materials and products for as long as possible.

There are four ways to make an economy more circular. Narrowing the loop means using fewer resources. Slowing it means reuse and repair. Closing it means {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}. The fourth is substituting renewable or less harmful inputs. Done worldwide, circularity could cut emissions by 22.8 billion tons, equal to 39% of global emissions in 2019, a large lever for {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}.

The idea is older than the name. In 1966 Kenneth Boulding wrote 'The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth'. It contrasted an open 'cowboy economy' with a closed one, and it is often cited as the idea's first expression. Pearce and Turner's 1990 book described a system where waste from extraction, production and consumption is turned back into inputs. The concept also draws on the study of industrial material flows, on design that copies nature, and on {{ref:nature-eecon-013}}. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation spread it in Europe and the Americas.

nature-eecon-032.title: Plastic pollution: cheap to make, slow to vanish
nature-eecon-032.text:
More than 900 marine species are affected by plastic pollution, the build-up of plastic objects and particles in the environment. Bottles, bags and microbeads all harm people, wildlife and habitats. Plastics are cheap and durable, so manufacturers favor them, but most resist natural breakdown and degrade slowly. Debris is sorted by size into micro-, meso- and macro-debris; macrodebris is larger than 20 mm.

Around 275 million tonnes of plastic waste is generated each year, and between 4.8 and 12.7 million tonnes of it is dumped into the sea. Packaging is the largest use, at 219 Mt as of 2024. Industry leaders knew in the early 1970s that most plastic would never be recycled, yet later ran a $50 million a year campaign saying it was. Governments most often target bags, by bans or fees, then cutlery and microbeads. Many academics and NGOs want a legally binding treaty to cap plastic production, a direct answer to this {{ref:nature-found-075}}.

nature-eecon-008.title: Industrial ecology: factories modeled on ecosystems
nature-eecon-008.text:
A natural {{ref:nature-found-015}} has no waste: what one organism discards, another uses. Industrial ecology takes that as a design model. It is the study of how materials and energy flow through industrial systems. It aims to move industry from open loops, where resources end as waste, to closed loops, where wastes become inputs for new processes.

The field was popularized in a 1989 Scientific American article by Robert Frosch and Nicholas Gallopoulos. They asked a simple question: why could one industry's outputs not be another's inputs? Today the field combines engineering, economics, sociology, toxicology and the natural sciences. Its research covers industrial metabolism, life-cycle assessment, eco-design, extended producer responsibility and {{ref:nature-eecon-018}}. Its principles now appear in circular economy policy, for example using waste heat from one process to run a cooler one.

nature-eecon-044.title: Resource recovery: treating waste as raw material
nature-eecon-044.text:
Lithium, cobalt and vanadium for electric vehicles and wind turbines can be pulled from industrial landfills and old mine wastes. That is resource recovery: using wastes as raw material to make valuable new products. It aims to cut waste and the need for landfill while getting the most value out of what is thrown away. It also delays the need to dig up fresh raw materials.

Recovery is one piece of a {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}, which minimizes both resource extraction and waste. It goes beyond {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} to include any way of winning value back from {{ref:nature-pol-064}} and industrial waste.

Its potential shrinks with time. Through manufacture, use and landfilling, materials are irreversibly mixed and diluted; physicists would say their entropy, their disorder, rises. The more scattered a material becomes, the harder it is to win back.

Some recovery is a sign of failure. Capturing landfill gas for energy counts as recovery, but it is a last resort, because the whole point is to avoid landfill altogether.

nature-eecon-022.title: The waste hierarchy: a pyramid of better and worse
nature-eecon-022.text:
In 1979 a Dutch member of parliament, Ad Lansink, proposed ranking ways of dealing with waste. 'Lansink's Ladder' became the waste hierarchy. It orders the options from the most to the least environmentally preferable, usually drawn as a pyramid. Its aim is to get the most practical benefit from products while generating the least waste.

The EU's 2008 Waste Framework Directive set five steps in order. Prevention comes first, then reuse, then recycling. Next is other recovery, including energy recovery. Safe disposal is the last resort. An early EU proposal had put recycling level with incineration; it was heavily criticized and replaced by the five-step version.

Applied well, the hierarchy can cut greenhouse gas emissions and other {{ref:nature-found-079}}, save energy and resources, create jobs and spur green technology.

It is a rule of thumb, not a law of nature. Looking at a product's whole life can justify breaking it. Replacing an old, inefficient washing machine is often better than keeping it, because most of its impact comes while it runs.

nature-eecon-057.title: Zero waste: designing waste out from the start
nature-eecon-057.text:
Only 9% of global plastic is currently recycled. Zero waste aims at a far bolder target: sending nothing to landfills, incinerators, oceans or anywhere else in the environment. It is a set of principles for preventing waste by redesigning how resources flow, so that all products are reused or repurposed.

The approach rejects managing waste at the end of the pipe. It calls for a 'whole systems' change in how materials move through society. That means products that are easy to take apart for {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}, durable and repairable, with minimal packaging. For households, Bea Johnson's '5 Rs' (refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle, rot) extend the familiar three. Many organizations and cities adopt the slogan, though, without pressing for its key changes.

nature-eecon-007.title: Dematerialization: doing more with less stuff
nature-eecon-007.text:
Cars weigh 30% less than in the early 1960s, and aluminium soda cans are six times lighter. Both are examples of dematerialization: making more goods, or meeting the same economic needs, with less material.

The shift can be absolute or relative. Absolute means a cut in total material use. Relative means less material per unit of economic output, such as {{ref:nature-econ-483}}, even if the total still rises. Products shed material in three ways. Optimizing means using less mass. Digitizing turns paper into an e-book. Servitizing means renting instead of selling.

The United States offers a striking case. Between 1977 and 2001 the material needed to meet Americans' needs fell from 1.18 to 1.08 trillion pounds, while population grew by 55 million.

Critics are not convinced the trend is real at a global scale. Extraction of six minerals and cement production grew faster than GDP from 1960 to 2019. Part of rich countries' dematerialization comes from moving material-hungry production to developing countries. Some critics say there is little evidence of global dematerialization at all, only regional shifts caused by that outsourcing. The question remains disputed, and it matters for whether {{ref:nature-econ-478}} can coexist with smaller demands on {{ref:nature-res-248}}.

nature-eecon-040.title: Does recycling pay? The economics of recycling
nature-eecon-040.text:
Virgin plastic resin costs 40 percent less than recycled resin. For many cities it is also cheaper to landfill household waste than to recycle it. Numbers like these fuel the economics of recycling, a dispute over whether recycling's economic and environmental benefits outweigh its costs.

Critics argue that collecting and trucking materials costs money and burns energy, enough to outweigh the savings in production. Supporters answer that comparing market prices alone leaves things out. Making new plastic causes extra pollution that nobody pays for, an {{ref:nature-found-031}}. Life cycle assessment can measure such hidden costs, and tools such as a carbon tax can build them into market prices.

How a program is set up matters too. Communities save money when recycling replaces their usual waste system rather than adding to it. The two sides still disagree over whether recycling's {{ref:nature-econ-114}} and energy use exceed its savings, and the answer may differ from place to place.

nature-eecon-050.title: The sharing economy: using what sits idle
nature-eecon-050.text:
The average car sits unused 95% of the time. The sharing economy puts such spare capacity to work. It is an economic system in which people share in making, distributing, trading and using goods and services, often through online platforms. It can be run by non-profits, like a lending library, or by companies for profit, such as Uber and Airbnb. By sharing, it can cut the number of goods that must be produced, and so reduce environmental harm.

There is no consensus on its definition, and its effects are disputed. Critics say platforms avoid taxes, regulation and insurance costs, and can push wages into a {{ref:nature-gov-150}}. Whether its workers are independent contractors or employees is still debated. So is whether its gains come from real efficiency or from dodging rules.

nature-eecon-004.title: Circular business models: profit from keeping things in use
nature-eecon-004.text:
A firm can make money by selling a product as a service, running a sharing platform or extending product life. These are circular business models: ways of earning a {{ref:nature-econ-409}} while keeping resources in use. They aim to use resources better, cut waste and create value for firms and customers. The key idea is to build loops that recapture value that would otherwise be lost.

Early talk centered on 're-X' steps such as recycling, {{ref:nature-eecon-043}}, reuse and recovery. Today four strategies are named. Narrowing loops uses fewer materials. Slowing loops relies on repair, reuse, resale and rental. Closing loops recycles into new production, and the fourth regenerates natural systems. Digital tools such as the internet of things, big data and AI are seen as key to scaling up. Hurdles remain in technology, consumer habits and profitability. Firms switching to secondhand raw materials do not necessarily cut short-term costs.

nature-eecon-003.title: Critiques of the circular economy: can loops really close?
nature-eecon-003.text:
Physics sets a ceiling on circularity. Under the second law of thermodynamics, scattered materials take energy to gather back up, and that energy rises steeply as the recycled share rises. Recovery can therefore never reach 100%. This is one of several critiques of the {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}: objections that it leaves growth unquestioned, ignores economics and thermodynamics, and neglects social justice.

The economic objection came from Zink and Geyer. They argued that supporters treat the world as an engineering system. They also questioned whether closing loops really prevents new primary production, or simply adds recycled material on top of it.

Growth is a third worry. Efficiency gains for each product can be swamped by growth in total consumption. Some scholars therefore call for a post-growth circular economy.

The fourth critique concerns fairness. Most circular economy plans do not ask who controls the technologies or how the costs and benefits are shared. That gap has prompted calls for a 'circular society'.

These questions are open. Scholars still dispute whether closing material loops actually displaces primary production, and whether circularity is compatible with growth at all.

nature-eecon-002.title: R-hierarchies: ranking refuse, reuse, recycle and the rest
nature-eecon-002.text:
In 2018 Reike and colleagues compared 69 different R hierarchies and found 38 distinct 're' words. R-hierarchies are ranked lists of 're-' actions, such as refuse, reduce, reuse, repair and recycle. They order circular strategies by how much value they keep or how much waste they avoid. They are probably inspired by the 1970s motto 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle', and they extend the logic of the {{ref:nature-eecon-022}} to the {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}.

Reike's team unified the jumble into a 10R framework. At the top sit refusing and reducing raw material use, because the best waste is the one never created. Next come reuse, repair, refurbishing, rebuilding to factory standard, and finding new uses, which keep a product or its parts working. Recycling ranks near the bottom, since it breaks products down to their materials. Lowest of all is energy recovery by incineration, which keeps only the heat.

nature-eecon-013.title: Cradle to cradle: materials as nutrients that circulate
nature-eecon-013.text:
The usual life of a product runs 'cradle to grave', from making to disposal. Cradle-to-cradle design plays on that phrase. It is a nature-inspired way of designing products and systems in which materials are treated as nutrients that circulate safely and endlessly, as they do in an {{ref:nature-found-015}}. The goal is systems that are not just efficient but essentially waste-free. It builds on John T. Lyle's regenerative design and can apply to cities, buildings, economies and social systems.

At Ford's River Rouge plant, a planted roof formed part of an $18 million rainwater system that saved Ford $30 million in mechanical treatment facilities. Today's recycling works against the idea. Sites usually crush whole products rather than take them apart. That makes recovering rare-earth elements and sorting alloys uneconomical. The name 'Cradle to Cradle' is a trademark of the consultancy MBDC. After criticism, MBDC handed its certification to an independent non-profit institute in 2012.

nature-eecon-055.title: Waste valorization: turning residues into value
nature-eecon-055.text:
Red mud from alumina production, mine tailings and even spent nuclear fuel can be turned into something useful. Waste valorization gives economic value to waste or residues by reusing or recycling them into useful materials. It usually means using the leftovers of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another, the core idea of {{ref:nature-eecon-008}}.

Industrial wastes suit it best. They are more consistent and predictable than household waste, so a factory can plan around them. Household rubbish varies from bin to bin.

Interest grew in the 1990s and 2000s for two reasons. Regulators tightened the rules on residues, making them costlier to dump. At the same time, ideas of sustainable development and the circular economy spread. Valorization is a close cousin of {{ref:nature-eecon-044}}, with the stress on the value created.

nature-eecon-043.title: Remanufacturing: rebuilt as good as new
nature-eecon-043.text:
A remanufactured machine should meet the same customer expectations as a new one. That promise sets remanufacturing apart from other recovery processes, which stop short of it. Remanufacturing rebuilds a used product to the original maker's specifications, from a mix of reused, repaired and new parts.

The process is thorough. A discarded product is taken fully apart. Usable parts are cleaned and refurbished. Then it is reassembled into a unit equal to new, and sometimes better. This goes further than simple {{ref:nature-pol-066}}.

The product may keep its identity or lose it. Photocopiers and toner cartridges are typical examples of the kinds of goods rebuilt this way.

The practice is still small. In 2020 it made up 2% of all US manufacturing and 1.9% in the EU. As a way of slowing the loop, it is one of the stronger tools of a {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}.

nature-eecon-053.title: Upcycling: making trash worth more than before
nature-eecon-053.text:
Before the Industrial Revolution, upcycling to repair goods was common. Mass production and a linear habit of throwing things away pushed it aside. Upcycling turns waste or unwanted products into new materials or products seen as having greater quality or value, such as artistic or environmental value.

It is a subset of {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} that adds value. Its opposite, {{ref:nature-eecon-015}}, turns waste into lower-quality products. Both words first appeared in print in a 1994 SalvoNEWS article.

Upcycling is a circular economy strategy. By raising a product's value and stretching its life through repair and new uses, it cuts resource use.

The same act can mean different things in different places. In poorer countries, upcycling often reflects a lack of access to new goods. In rich countries, it more often reflects concern for the environment.
